title: Entitlement Evaluation at Request Time: Hierarchical Permission Graphs, Cache Invalidation, and the Stale-Grant Hazard
description: How permission graph traversal, Redis-backed entitlement caches, and invalidation contracts interact under real multi-tenant authorization workloads.
linkedin_post:
Stale authorization grants are one of the quietest failure modes in multi-tenant systems. You revoke a role at 14:02. The user's entitlement cache expires at 14:58. For 56 minutes, your authorization layer says yes to a question that should be no.

This isn't a tuning problem. Shortening the TTL trades one approximation for another. The root cause is using TTL-based expiry as an invalidation strategy for a correctness-critical data structure.

My latest article covers the full production design:

→ Why permission graphs can't be safely flattened at login time
→ How a version fence in Redis eliminates the stale-grant window without querying the permission store on every request
→ The thundering herd problem on tenant-wide revocations — and a per-principal recompute lock pattern in Go that serializes the work without global blocking
→ Why deny semantics must be materialized into the cached entitlement set, not recomputed on evaluation
→ Cross-region tradeoffs when the fence lives in an async replica

The key insight: the stale window is closed by replacing TTL expiry with event-driven fence updates. The fence is written atomically with the permission-store mutation; the next request in that tenant sees the version mismatch and triggers a recompute. Propagation latency drops from minutes to the change stream lag — typically under 100ms.

The article includes Go examples for the pipeline-based fence+cache read, the SetNX recompute lock, and deny-aware grant matching.

If you're building RBAC for systems where revocation latency has a real security boundary, the design decisions here are worth examining carefully.
